sources.news_title: Trump Cuts Irish Whiskey Tariffs Because ‘Everyone’s Been Bugging Me’ About It
sources.text:
By Darlene Superville and Jill Lawless
DOONBEG, Ireland (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Sunday at the close of a golf tournament in Ireland that he plans to remove a 10% tariff on Irish whiskey.
Trump said during the trophy ceremony for the Irish Open that he had been asked about the issue by everyone, including Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin and even some of the golfers. Irish Open winner Shane Lowry was among them, Trump said.
“Everybody’s been bugging me” to do it, the Republican president said. “And I said, ‘On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off’” of Irish whiskey.
Trending
Irish whiskey currently faces the standard tariff imposed by Trump on most imports from the European Union, which was reduced from 15% to 10% in July.
Trump announced in April that he was lifting certain tariffs on U.K. whiskey, which includes Scotch and spirits made in Northern Ireland, creating an imbalance with Ireland.
Trump’s surprise announcement was met with loud whistling and cheers from the crowd of spectators. Details on how soon the tariff would be lifted were not immediately available.
Chris Swonger, president & CEO of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, called Trump’s announcement “another positive step toward reducing barriers to spirits trade” and said everyone would benefit from it during the coming holidays.
“As U.S. hospitality businesses enter the critical holiday season, this action will provide a welcome boost for retailers, restaurants, consumers and the American economy,” Swonger said.
In May, the Irish Whiskey Association called for the tariffs to be removed, arguing that such a step would help many U.S. companies with Irish products in their portfolios and avoid uncertainty for consumers.
Trump said on April 30 that he gave the United Kingdom a tariff break on whiskey after King Charles III and Queen Camilla visited the White House. “The King and Queen got me to do something that nobody else was able to do, without hardly even asking!” Trump posted on social media.
The Scotch Whisky Association said July 24 that the zero-tariff policy had come into effect.

sources.news_title: 'Everybody's been bugging me' about it | President Trump says he's lifting tariff on Irish whiskey
Major update after Donald Trump announces he'll remove tariffs on Irish whiskey
sources.text:
Irish whiskey exports to the United States are set to become tariff-free after Donald Trump announced the removal of the current levy on the product.
The US President confirmed the move during his visit to Ireland over the weekend, with the concession applying to Irish whiskey but – crucially – it has now been confirmed it will not apply to the wider European Union.
It means Irish whiskey will receive the same tariff-free treatment as Scotch and whiskey produced in Northern Ireland – which had already been granted a tariff exemption as part of a deal with the UK.
Irish whiskey exports to the US were worth around €450 million last year.
The Irish Whiskey Association has welcomed the announcement, but says it will continue working with officials in both the EU and US to secure a return to zero tariffs across all drinks exports.
Director Eoin Ó Catháin said a zero-for-zero trading arrangement remained the preferred outcome.
‘The message we have had consistently, and this has been shared with our colleagues in Brussels, is that the zero-for-zero trading arrangement is best for all,’ he said.
Mr. Ó Catháin said the industry had expected movement on tariffs at some point, but the timing of the announcement came as a surprise.
‘I think we were expecting an announcement at some point, but it came on the green of the 18th hole. We weren’t really expecting it at that point, but we’re delighted it came through.’
President Donald Trump announced the decision during the Irish Open trophy presentation at his Doonbeg resort.
The 10% tariff had formed part of wider US duties applied to EU wine and spirit exports.

sources.news_title: Trump Announces End to 10 Percent Tariff on Irish Whiskey › American Greatness
sources.text:
President Donald Trump announced Sunday that the United States will eliminate its 10 percent tariff on Irish whiskey, offering a significant trade concession to Ireland following repeated appeals from Irish officials and the country’s spirits industry.
Trump made the surprise announcement during the trophy ceremony at the Irish Open, held at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg.
“Everybody’s been bugging me” about the tariff, Trump told the crowd, adding that some professional golfers had raised the issue with him.
“And I said, ‘On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off’” Irish whiskey, Trump said.
The announcement drew cheers and whistles from spectators. Trump did not provide a date for when the tariff exemption would take effect.
Irish whiskey has been subject to the 10 percent U.S. import tariff applied to many European Union products. Trump previously exempted certain British spirits, including Scotch whisky and whiskey produced in Northern Ireland, from U.S. tariffs.
The Irish Whiskey Association had pressed the administration to provide similar treatment to whiskey produced in the Republic of Ireland, arguing that tariffs hurt producers on both sides of the Atlantic. Many American spirits companies own or distribute Irish whiskey brands.
Trump said his decision followed appeals from several people, including Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin and Irish golfer Shane Lowry, who won the Irish Open on Sunday.
The move would restore an important tariff advantage for one of Ireland’s best-known exports and remove an additional cost for U.S. importers bringing Irish whiskey into the American market.
The administration has not yet released details explaining how or when the tariff exemption will be implemented.
Trump’s decision comes as his administration continues to use tariffs as leverage in trade negotiations with major U.S. trading partners. A February presidential proclamation imposed a temporary 10 percent surcharge on most imported goods, subject to specified exemptions.

sources.news_title: Teetotal Trump's strange weakness for whiskey
sources.text:
Shane Lowry holed a 30-foot birdie putt on the 18th at Doonbeg on Sunday and began stretching his arms out before the ball dropped, a fitting end to a week in which he won the Amgen Irish Open by a record 11 shots.
Donald Trump, president of the United States, who just so happens to own the golf resort, was watching from a box seat. He came down to present the trophy.
Then, cameras still running, Trump, as easy as swapping clubs, changed the subject from golf to tariffs.
People had been asking him about the 10 percent duty on Irish whiskey, Trump explained. The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, in Dublin the day before. Lowry too. More or less everyone.
"Everybody’s been bugging me," Trump said, and announced that on behalf of the U.S., he was taking it off. The crowd erupted. The famous luck of the Irish had paid off, or perhaps it was the charm. Choose your preferred cliché.
The Irish Whiskey Association puts the annual U.S. export value at roughly €450 million ($519 million). Trump gave no implementation date, so the Irish are on a promise. When he made the same about Scotch, it took nearly three months to take effect.
Interestingly, the man making it says he never drinks, citing the warnings of his late older brother, Fred, who died aged 42 of alcoholism. Still, alcohol has been a persistent fixture of this famous teetotaler's trade policy, used as tool to both reward and punish those with whom he is in dispute.
On April 30, the final day of King Charles III’s state visit, Trump said he would scrap the tariff on British whisky—“in honor of the King and Queen who just left," he told reporters, adding that they had got him to do something others had failed to.
The pledge took effect July 24, and Scotch, whose American market was worth £933 million ($1.25 billion) in 2025, now enters at zero.
Twice this year, then, Trump has publicly promised a whiskey carve-out after somebody he likes asked for one. Sláinte, lads!
The tempting conclusion is that he is a soft touch for whiskey. Flattered by monarchs, charmed by sportsmen, and sentimental about a drink he never tried.
Really, whiskey has become a recurring vehicle for personalized trade diplomacy, a category of product nationally branded and culturally significant in a way steel and semiconductors are not.
Whiskey, or whisky depending where you are and what you’re drinking, enjoy organized industries and famous champions, and is a small enough industry against a national trade balance that a crowd-pleasing carve-out need not reopen the wider tariff war.
But there is much more going on than a whispered appeal into Trump’s ear.
The U.K. government credits the Scotch exemption to sustained, government-led engagement with Trump. Scotland’s first minister gave a nod to the King, but also a wider campaign by Scottish ministers and the industry.
The Irish Whiskey Association had been pressing publicly for the same treatment since the day after the Scotch decision, pointing out that a single protected product was attracting two different U.S. tariffs depending on which side of the Irish border it was distilled.
And the Irish rate had already fallen: 15 percent under the 2025 regime, then 10 after a broad round of U.S. tariff action in July covering 60 trading partners. The line was moving before anyone teed off at Doonbeg.
Yet alcohol keeps surfacing in unusually public episodes of Trump’s trade diplomacy, good and bad.
In March 2025, when Brussels proposed a 50 percent tariff on American whiskey in retaliation for steel and aluminum duties, Trump threatened 200 percent on European wine and spirits unless it was dropped.
Eurostat put all EU alcoholic-beverage exports to the U.S. at €8.9 billion ($10.3 billion) in 2024. The French needed a very stiff drink when Trump dropped that particular bomb on their economy.
It isn’t just Europe whose booze industry thrives or survives by Trump’s bottle diplomacy.
After Canadian provinces pulled American drink from their state-run liquor systems, Trump, angry, reached for the bottle.
Or, more specifically, Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930—a dormant provision permitting retaliation against discriminatory treatment—and built a punitive regime on it.
His July 20 proclamation on alcohol, one of three issued that day alongside dairy and vehicles, found that U.S. alcohol exports to Canada had fallen from about $718 million to $137 million, roughly 81 percent.
Fifty percent duties followed, delayed three days while Ottawa talked, then imposed on August 22 after the White House said Canada had "reneged" on its commitment.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney claims it was he who suspended the talks, saying late changes to the American terms were "unfair, uneconomic."
Trump went further on September 8, ordering specified Canadian alcoholic beverages excluded from importation from the end of the month. Five days later, he stood on a green in Clare and promised to lift the Irish duty.
What makes the category of product so useful in trade diplomacy is that its reciprocity is already physical.
Scottish distilleries buy around $270 million of used Kentucky bourbon barrels a year, and the Irish industry describes Ireland as the EU’s largest importer of American oak, with most Irish whiskey maturing in ex-bourbon casks.
Scotland’s first minister called the July outcome "zero-for-zero," an arrangement with an economic logic independent of royal access. But it has not always run this way. In Trump’s first term whiskey was collateral rather than favor.
After Washington won its WTO case over Airbus subsidies in 2019, single-malt Scotch and Scotch whisky liqueurs took 25 percent duties under countermeasures covering roughly $7.5 billion of EU goods.
In December 2020 certain nonsparkling wines, cognac and grape brandies from France and Germany were added. The president who once used European spirits as leverage in an aircraft dispute now publicly announces whiskey exemptions.
We still don’t know what instrument implements the Doonbeg pledge, or when it will arrive. Nor do we yet know if anything is moving the other way—an EU concession, or a separate Irish commitment in return, for example.
The EU does not let individual member nations negotiate bilateral trade agreements. So where does this leave the rest of the booze produced by EU member states? If it applies for Irish whiskey, why not French liquor?
Until those answers exist, what happened on the 18th green is a promise rather than a policy, and the pattern it belongs to is an open question rather than a closed conclusion.
A president who has never had a drink has now twice put whiskey at the front of a public trade announcement, at the request of people whose names everyone knows. Whether that is how policy is made or merely announced is not yet clear.
For now, it’s time for a drink. But Trump's is a Diet Coke.

sources.news_title: Sláinte! Trump Scraps 10% Tariff on All Irish Whiskey as Parting Gift
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump bade farewell to Ireland on Sunday, ending his two-day visit by announcing he will remove tariffs from Irish whiskey.
AP reports Trump used the trophy ceremony for the Irish Open to reveal he had been asked about the issue by everyone, including Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin and even some of the golfers.
The crowd erupted into cheers and a round of applause at the news with Irish Open winner Shane Lowry among them.
The surprise trade move came a day after the U.S. president stirred controversy by calling for Irish reunification, as Breitbart News reported.
“Everybody’s been bugging me” to do it, the Republican president said. “And I said, ‘On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off’” of Irish whiskey.
Irish whiskey currently faces the standard 10 percent tariff imposed by Trump on most imports from the European Union, which was reduced from 15 percent to 10 percent in July.
Trump announced in April that he was lifting certain tariffs on U.K. whiskey, which includes Scotch and spirits made in Northern Ireland, creating an imbalance with Ireland, as international trade negotiation give-and-take go on.
He gave the UK its a tariff break after King Charles III and Queen Camilla visited the White House.
Director of the Irish Whiskey Association Eoin Ó Catháin rejoiced, saying the Irish whiskey sector is “delighted” with the announcement, RTE 100 noted. He said:
The U.S. is our biggest market, it represents thousands of jobs, millions in investments and it has been under pressure, I suppose, over the last year and a bit because of that tariff.
We’re delighted to see it removed.
We’ll continue to work with all of our colleagues in the U.S., in Brussels, here in Dublin to ensure this full tariff liberalisation will take place.
Irish Open champion Shane Lowry joked Irish distillers better send him a cheque following Trump’s announcement, the RTE 100 report went on to note.
Speaking at a press conference after receiving his Irish Open title, the golfer said he had attended a dinner with Trump but the president had not told him he was changing his plans to stay to watch him win, as had been suggested.
“He also announced he was removing tariffs on whiskey because of me … so distillers better start sending me a cheque,” he laughed.
Asked whether he had put pressure on the Republican president to lift the Irish whiskey tariffs, Lowry joked “I’ll take credit for that.”
The Distilled Spirits Council of the United States also welcomed the move.
“This announcement is another positive step toward reducing barriers to spirits trade,” Chris Swonger, the council’s president and chief executive, said in a statement.

sources.news_title: Trump Backs United Ireland, Lifts Whiskey Tariffs
sources.text:
President Trump used the final day of his two-day Ireland visit to double down on his call for a united Ireland and announce the removal of tariffs on Irish whiskey, moves that drew both praise from local business owners and protests from critics.
Speaking to reporters at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare, after watching Irish golfer Shane Lowry tee off at the Irish Open on Sunday, Trump restated the position he first voiced a day earlier during meetings with Taoiseach Micheál Martin in Dublin. BBC News NI reported that Trump framed the idea as common sense rather than provocation.
"I've always loved the people of Ireland. It just seems to me you have Northern Ireland and Ireland," Trump told reporters. "It seems that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together."
He called the remark "a fairly routine comment" and added: "That's only my opinion, and by the way many people agree." Asked whether he held similar views on Scottish independence, Trump sidestepped. "I won't talk about Scotland yet I will save that," he said.
Taoiseach Martin, who had met with Trump in Dublin on Saturday, did not distance himself from the remarks. Instead he characterized the response as overblown.
"He would make the point this is his view. He believes unity is the logical way for the island to be configured and organised."
Martin told reporters Trump's position "shouldn't be a surprise" and said some of the reaction amounted to "an overreaction." He added that Trump simply "takes a different sort of perspective on things." The comments stood in contrast to the sharper pushback from London, where Trump's Dublin remarks had already drawn criticism from British officials.
Trump was also asked about remarks attributed to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who indicated there would be no poll on Irish unity until a majority in Northern Ireland appeared likely to vote in favor. Trump brushed the point aside: "Everybody says that and then things happen."
The bigger economic headline came during the trophy ceremony. After handing the winner's trophy to Lowry, Trump announced that he would lift tariffs on Irish whiskey. Irish whiskey distilled in the Republic of Ireland currently faces a 15 percent tariff, the standard rate applied to EU goods entering the United States.
The announcement followed a move Trump made in May to remove tariffs on all UK-made whiskey. That earlier cut, however, created an unintended gap. Northern Ireland distilleries that bottle whiskey produced by the Great Northern Distillery in Dundalk, County Louth, which sits in the Republic, were classified as EU rather than UK producers. They could not benefit from the UK tariff removal. Whether Sunday's announcement resolves that cross-border wrinkle remains unclear.
Trump has used tariff policy as a signature tool throughout his presidency, imposing sharp levies on Canadian alcohol imports while simultaneously cutting duties on products from allied nations when it suits broader diplomatic goals.
No formal executive order or written directive was cited in connection with the whiskey announcement. It came as a verbal declaration during a public speech, a format Trump has used before to signal policy shifts on trade.
While protesters and critics dominated international coverage, the view inside Doonbeg itself ran in the opposite direction. Local business owners described Trump's golf resort as the economic lifeline of a rural community that would otherwise be fading.
Seoirse Comerford, who owns the Comerford bar in the village, called the tournament "unbelievable" and laid out what the resort means in plain terms.
"Most rural villages in west Clare are all dying a death, young people going away to college, they don't come back. Like there's over 300 people employed up there at the golf course, it's a big boost to the local economy. You've got big companies in Dublin, like Intel, the golf course is our Intel down here."
Martin Kelly, another local businessman, echoed the sentiment. "It's a massive employer here to be honest with you," Kelly said. "There's nothing else about here at that scale; they're very decent people to work for, they're very fair." He said locals were "very proud" the tournament was taking place in Doonbeg and called the village "very fortunate" to have the course.
Those voices rarely make it into the international press cycle, but they represent the people who actually live with the day-to-day consequences of whether a major employer stays or goes. The resort's role as a jobs engine in west Clare is not abstract to them, it is the difference between a village that holds together and one that hollows out.
Opposition to Trump's visit was far larger in Dublin, where more than 10,000 people marched through the city on Saturday. By Sunday, about 100 protesters had gathered in Doonbeg, a sharp drop-off that reflected both geography and logistics.
Rev. Steven Foster, a Methodist minister from Galway, was among those who made the trip. He told BBC News NI he felt compelled to show up in person.
"I'm here because Trump is the exact opposite of everything I stand for as a follower of Jesus. As a church leader, it's important for me to be visible, and the church needs to be visible in this regard."
Foster argued that the "type of welcome he has been given sends out a terrible message." Irish police, the Gardaí, moved a small crowd from the president's hotel in Doonbeg, RTÉ reported. The situation never escalated beyond that.
Three women were arrested Saturday evening for trespassing on the golf links and appeared at a special sitting of Ennis District Court. No further details about the charges or the court's outcome were reported. The logistical complexity of presidential travel always raises the security stakes at events like these, and the arrests underscored how seriously Irish authorities treated the perimeter.
Trump's two-day swing through Ireland packed both diplomatic and economic messaging into a compact itinerary. Saturday brought the Dublin meeting with Martin and the initial united Ireland remarks. Sunday delivered the tariff announcement, the trophy ceremony, and a second round of comments reinforcing the same position on Irish unity.
The whiskey tariff cut fits a broader pattern. Trump has repeatedly used targeted trade concessions, and targeted trade penalties, as instruments of bilateral diplomacy. He opened the door to tariff-free beef from South America under similar circumstances, pairing economic sweeteners with political objectives during foreign engagements.
Whether the Irish whiskey announcement translates into a formal order, and whether it resolves the cross-border classification problem that left Northern Ireland distilleries in limbo after the UK tariff cut, are open questions. The Great Northern Distillery in Dundalk produces whiskey under licence for brands across the island. Its product crosses the border before it reaches a bottle, and, under current rules, that crossing determines which tariff schedule applies.
For now, the announcement stands as a verbal commitment made from a trophy stage in County Clare. The Irish whiskey industry will be watching for the paperwork.
Ten thousand marchers in Dublin got the headlines. Three hundred workers in Doonbeg got the jobs. The people who have to live with the results rarely get to set the terms of the debate, but they know which one pays the bills.

sources.news_title: Trump pledges to remove US tariff on Irish whiskey
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump has said he would remove the American tariff on Irish whiskey, announcing the decision on September 13 at the close of a two-day visit to Ireland.
He made the announcement on the 18th green at the Amgen Irish Open, played at his Doonbeg golf resort in County Clare, western Ireland. Minutes earlier he had presented the winner’s trophy to Irish golfer Shane Lowry.
Trump said he had discussed the duty with Taoiseach Micheál Martin and with Lowry, and that others had been pressing him on it.
“I am going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey,” he told a cheering crowd.
He gave no date for the change. Whiskey distilled in the Republic of Ireland currently enters the United States at 10 per cent.
That rate is not specific to Ireland. It applies to European Union wine and spirits generally under the EU-US trade framework agreed in 2025, which capped most duties at 15 per cent before a revision in July covering 60 trading partners brought wine and spirits down to 10 per cent.
Trade policy is an exclusive competence of the European Commission, which negotiated that framework on behalf of all member states.
Because Irish whiskey is a single geographical indication covering the whole island, the change would also reach distillers in Northern Ireland. Those producers had been left out of the removal of duties on UK-made whisky earlier this year, as all-island supply chains meant much of their output counted as Irish, according to BBC News.
The Irish Whiskey Association welcomed the announcement. Its director, Eoin Ó Catháin, said: “Nothing exemplifies the US-Ireland trade relationship better than Irish whiskey.”
The association said it would keep pressing its EU and US counterparts for a return to zero-for-zero terms on all drinks exports.
Tánaiste and Finance Minister Simon Harris called it “a welcome announcement of economic significance”. He said it reflected 18 months of engagement with the US administration.
The American market is worth between €400 million and €420 million a year to the sector. It took 38 per cent of Irish whiskey exports in 2025, down from 49 per cent in 2023, on Bord Bia figures cited by the association.
Irish distillers had cut back sharply under the duty, many pausing production during 2025.
The tariff announcement was not the main takeaway from the trip. Trump used both days to back Irish unification, saying it would be natural to put Ireland and Northern Ireland together and dismissing the diplomatic reaction as routine.
He met Martin in Dublin on September 12 and also saw Irish President Catherine Connolly.
Ireland holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union until the end of December.

sources.news_title: US will scrap Irish whisky tariff, Trump says
sources.text:
US will scrap Irish whisky tariff, Trump says
The announcement comes several months after the United States decreased the tariff by 5 percent.
While in Ireland attending a golf tournament at the golf course he owns in Doonbeg in County Clare, US President Donald Trump said the US will repeal a 10 percent tariff on Irish whisky, a duty that currently falls under those imposed on all European Union wine and spirit exports to the United States.
“Everybody’s been bugging me” to do it, the president said at a trophy ceremony. “And I said, ‘On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off [Irish whisky].'”
Irish whisky producers have been navigating the tariffs levied by the Trump administration on European Union imports for over a year, as part of the administration’s broader trade and import clampdown.
Trump announced a zero-tariff policy for spirits from the United Kingdom in late April, removing duties on Scotch and Northern Irish whisky following a royal visit from the UK’s King Charles III and Queen Camilla.
“The King and Queen got me to do something that nobody else was able to do, without hardly even asking!” Trump posted on social media at the time.
The Scotch Whisky Association said July 24 that the zero-tariff policy had come into effect, calling it “welcome news for businesses on both sides of the Atlantic” that would provide “greater confidence to invest, grow exports, and support jobs and communities”.
In May, the Irish Whiskey Association (IWA) also pressed for tariff elimination to shield US spirit portfolios and consumers from market volatility, while buttressing domestic companies handling Irish brands.
In July, the administration dropped an original 15 percent tariff to 10 percent.
The IWA welcomed the announcement and said it would continue to work with its EU and US counterparts to secure a return to the zero-for-zero tariff arrangement for all drinks exports.
“Nothing exemplifies the US-Ireland trade relationship better than Irish Whiskey,” IWA Director Eoin O Caithain said in a statement, adding that the lobby group looked forward to seeing the announcement fully implemented.
Trump’s sudden announcement at the tournament’s close triggered a chorus of whistles and cheers from the crowd of spectators. Details on how soon the tariff would be lifted were not immediately available.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump makes unexpected announcement during Irish Open trophy presentation
sources.text:
Donald Trump makes unexpected announcement during Irish Open trophy presentation
The U.S. President told the crowd at Trump Doonbeg that he would remove tariffs on Irish whiskey after speaking with Shane Lowry and Taoiseach Micheál Martin.
Donald Trump sparked one of the biggest reactions of the Irish Open weekend when he announced he would remove U.S. tariffs on Irish whiskey during the presentation ceremony at Trump Doonbeg.
The United States President had just handed Shane Lowry the Irish Open trophy when he turned his attention to the issue of tariffs, revealing that both Taoiseach Micheál Martin and the newly crowned champion had raised the matter with him.
Trump told the crowd gathered around the 18th green that he had been repeatedly asked to intervene.
“Everyone has been bugging me saying, ‘Would you do me a favour? It’s so unfair what’s going on. Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey?’” Trump said.
“And I said on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey.”
The response was immediate.
The announcement was greeted by loud cheers and applause from the crowd at Doonbeg, turning what had already been a memorable Irish Open presentation into an unexpected political and commercial announcement.
Trump had discussed the issue with Martin during their meeting at Farmleigh, with the Taoiseach understood to have asked the U.S. President to address the tariff imposed on Irish whiskey.
Watch Trump's announcement here:
Lowry, meanwhile, was more than happy to claim some of the credit.
Speaking afterwards, the two-time Irish Open champion joked that Irish distillers now owed him for his alleged role in Trump's decision.
“He also announced he was removing tariffs on whiskey because of me... so distillers better start sending me a cheque,” Lowry said.
When asked whether he had put pressure on Trump to make the change, Lowry added with a smile: “I’ll take credit for that.”
Record-breaking week for Lowry
The tariff announcement provided an unusual ending to what had been an extraordinary week for Lowry.
The Offaly man produced the most dominant performance in Irish Open history, finishing 23-under par and a remarkable 11 shots clear of the field.
That's a record-breaking margin in Irish Open history on the European Tour.
It was his second victory in the tournament, 17 years after he stunned the golf world by winning the Irish Open as a fresh-faced amateur in 2009.
The victory was also the seventh of Lowry's DP World Tour career and his first in exactly four years.
Lowry revealed that he had dinner with Trump on Saturday evening, although he said the U.S. President had not told him that he intended to remain at Doonbeg to watch his final round.
Rory McIlroy also attended the dinner.
The tariff issue has been an important one for the Irish whiskey industry.
Irish whiskey exported to the U.S. has been subject to a 10% tariff, leaving producers at a disadvantage to Scotch and Northern Irish whiskey, which currently face no equivalent tariff.
Any removal of the charge would therefore represent a significant boost for Irish whiskey producers.
The industry has continued to expand despite the challenges created by global trade disputes and changing tariff arrangements.
Recent figures from the Irish Whiskey Association showed that Irish whiskey export volumes to the EU had risen by 21.5% over the previous four years.
For Lowry, though, the day's headline belonged to his golf.
And after lifting the Irish Open trophy in front of a home crowd, he left Doonbeg with an extra reason to believe he had made an impact beyond the fairways.

sources.news_title: Trump scraps tariffs on Irish whiskey ‘on behalf of the United States of America’
sources.text:
US president Donald Trump made the surprise announcement that he would remove tariffs from Irish whiskey at the end of his two-day visit to Ireland.
It came shortly before he presented golfer Shane Lowry with the winner’s trophy after he triumphed in the Irish Open tournament at Trump’s golf resort in Doonbeg, Co Clare.
Irish whiskey was impacted as part of wide-ranging tariffs the Trump administration imposed on imports from the European Union and elsewhere.
Those on Irish whiskey were as high as 15 per cent last year, but that was subsequently reduced to 10 per cent.
READ MORE
It is understood Taoiseach Micheál Martin raised the issue with Trump during their meeting at Farmleigh on Saturday.
As he wrapped up his address to the crowd at the Irish Open, Trump said: “I want to mention one thing [the] Taoiseach and I talked about it, and Shane [Lowry] talked about it.
“Everybody’s been bugging me. They’re saying, ‘Will you do me a favour, it’s so unfair what’s going on. Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey?’
“And I said, on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off.”
The Irish Whiskey Association (IWA) quickly welcomed the announcement. Director Eoin Ó Catháin said: “Nothing exemplifies the US-Ireland trade relationship better than Irish whiskey.”
Exports to the US were worth €450 million in 2025, he said, while Irish distillers purchased €80 million worth of US whiskey casks.
“This relationship represents thousands of jobs and millions in investment on both sides of the Atlantic, and the return to tariff-free trade for our Irish whiskey distillers will strengthen this success and lead to further growth and investment.”
Tanaiste Simon Harris said the announcement was of economic significance and reflected the importance of the economic relationship between Ireland and the US. Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke said the US was a “vital market for our many quality local distillers across the country”, and the move would protect jobs.
At the post-tournament press conference, Lowry was asked about Trump’s remarks that the golfer had been among those with whom he had discussed whiskey tariffs. Lowry joked: “Irish distillers better be sending me a cheque soon. That must be worth a few quid to them.”
Meanwhile, the Taoiseach defended the manner in which he raised the issue of Gaza with Trump, including how he had not referred to what had happened in the Palestinian enclave as genocide.
People Before Profit TD Paul Murphy accused the Taoiseach of an “abject failure to challenge Trump” on the issue. Sinn Féin MEP Kathleen Funchion – who joined protesters near Trump’s golf resort in Doonbeg on Sunday – argued that the Irish people “would have liked for Micheál Martin to be a lot stronger” on Gaza and the “upholding of international law and accountability for Israel”.
Martin said his main focus was “accelerating getting more aid to Gaza” and that this was the “key issue now for the Palestinians”. He said he had received a thank you message “immediately afterwards” from the Palestinian ambassador.
Martin also mentioned Ireland’s intervention in the International Court of Justice (ICJ) case taken by South Africa alleging genocide by Israel in Gaza and said: “I took that decision with the Government some time back and we have been very consistent as a country in relation to the Middle East and in relation to the Palestinian question.”
He said the US president “undertook to do everything he possibly could to get aid into Gaza and particularly the Irish contribution in respect of that.”
Asked whether he told Trump that what was happening in Gaza was genocide, Martin said: “No, I didn’t use that term specifically,” while denying he had changed his language on the issue when meeting Trump.
The US president’s whirlwind visit to Ireland ended on Sunday. Trump praised the hospitality of the Irish people he had experienced, while also remarking that some were among the “most vicious bastards” he has done business with during his two-day visit.
He said Irish-based medical companies had “fleeced” the US by not paying taxes there.
Following his arrival in Ireland on Saturday, Trump first visited the Phoenix Park, where he met President Catherine Connolly in Áras an Uachtaráin and then the Taoiseach in Farmleigh House. Afterwards, he spoke at an event in the residence of the US ambassador Edward Walsh at Deerfield, also in the Phoenix Park.
The president then flew on Air Force One to Doonbeg, where he watched the final two days of the Irish Open.

sources.text:
On foreign land but home turf, Donald Trump presented the Irish Open trophy to Shane Lowry at the president’s Doonbeg golf course. He also presented a farewell gift: the elimination of tariffs on Irish whiskey.
“I want to mention one thing. Taoiseach and I talked about it, and Shane talked about it, and everybody’s been bugging me. They’re saying, ‘Would you do me a favor? It’s so unfair what’s going on. Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey?’” Trump said.
“And I said, on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off,” Trump continued, as the crowd erupted.
While not a drinker himself, Trump presented the show of good faith at the end of his quick visit to Ireland — where he made controversial comments voicing support for Irish unification, met with Irish President Catherine Connolly and Taoiseach Micheál Martin, and became the first sitting president to attend the Irish Open.

Chris Swonger, president and CEO of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, welcomed the move, saying in a statement it marks “another positive step toward reducing barriers to spirits trade.”

After Trump’s meetings in Dublin on Saturday, the news was dominated by his support for Irish unification, a controversial issue, while Sunday, he turned the attention to whiskey tariffs.
Trump said Saturday that he discussed trade with Martin at their bilateral meeting and emphasized the US’ “big relationship with Ireland,” which he said will “continue stronger than ever.”

“In many ways, the last four days reflects also the very strong relationship, the strength of an enduring relationship between the United States of America and Ireland. We are tied together by history, by family, by friendship,” he added.

He spent the weekend at his own golf club — greeted with chants of “U-S-A” in the packed members bar on Saturday night and cheered on while presenting the trophy on Sunday.
“We’re so proud of the whole Doonbeg, and, frankly, Ireland itself has been so incredible, so inviting,” Trump said.

sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump said he would lift tariffs on Irish whiskey during comments made at the end of a golf tournament in Ireland.
Trump had been facing questions about the current 10 percent tariff imposed on Irish whiskey.
During the trophy ceremony for the Irish Open, Trump said that he had been asked about the issue by everyone, including some of the golfers.
“Everybody’s been bugging me” about the tariff, Trump said. “And I said, ‘On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey.’”
The tariff is imposed on imports from the European Union. Trump announced in April that he was removing certain tariffs on U.K. whiskey, which includes Scotch and spirits made in Northern Ireland.
The crowd cheered when Trump made the announcement.
The Irish Whiskey Association had called for the tariff to be removed in April after Trump announced an exemption for whiskey produced in the United Kingdom. The Irish Whiskey Association said Irish whiskey exports to the United States were valued at about $525 million annually, based on the current exchange rate.
Removing the tariff would benefit U.S. companies carrying premium Irish products, reduce uncertainty for Americans, and support the barrel-making industry in Kentucky, Tennessee, and other states, the association said. Ireland is the European Union’s largest importer of American oak casks, with most Irish whiskey matured in barrels previously used to produce bourbon.
The association also noted that Irish whiskey is a protected product encompassing the entire island. That meant the same product faced different U.S. tariffs depending on whether it was produced in Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom, or the Republic of Ireland, an EU member.
Trump said he would remove a tariff on whiskey produced in Scotland after King Charles III and Queen Camilla’s White House visit in April.
“In Honor of the King and Queen of the United Kingdom, who have just left the White House, soon headed back to their wonderful Country, I will be removing the Tariffs and Restrictions on Whiskey having to do with Scotland’s ability to work with the Commonwealth of Kentucky on Whiskey and Bourbon, two very important Industries within Scotland and Kentucky,” Trump posted on Truth Social on April 30.
“People have wanted to do this for a long time, in that there had been great Inter-Country Trade, especially having to do with the Wooden Barrels used. The King and Queen got me to do something that nobody else was able to do, without hardly even asking! A wonderful Honor to have them both in the U.S.A.”

sources.news_title: Trump makes announcement on whiskey tariffs as he brings Irish visit to a close
sources.text:
Donald Trump made a surprise announcement that he was removing US tariffs on Irish whiskey as he brought his two-day visit to Ireland to a close.
Crowds cheered the US President as he made the announcement on the 18th green during the prizewinning ceremony at the Amgen Irish Open at his Doonbeg golf resort in Co Clare.
Shortly after, the US president left Shannon Airport aboard Air Force One to fly back to Washington.
Earlier, Mr Trump doubled down on his comments in support of Irish unity, saying it was “one of the naturals of all time”.
Speaking on the second day of his trip to Ireland, Mr Trump also dismissed the diplomatic backlash to his remarks, which have dominated his trip.
However, he refused to answer questions about a timeline for a border poll and also avoided a question about Scottish independence.
Irish premier Micheál Martin said there had been an “overreaction” to the president’s remarks.
On Sunday the President, wearing a white baseball cap with USA written on the front, presented the Irish Open trophy to winner Shane Lowry from Co Offaly.
He told the crowd he had discussed whiskey tariffs with Taoiseach Micheál Martin and with golfer Lowry.
He said: “Everybody’s been bugging me.
“They are saying would you do me a favour? It’s so unfair what’s going on.
“Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey and I said, on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey.”
Whiskey made in the Republic of Ireland sold into the US is subject to a 10% tariff. Whiskey made in Northern Ireland or elsewhere in the UK has no tariff.
Read More
Lowry joked at a post-tournament press conference: “Irish distillers better be sending me a cheque soon – that must be worth a few quid with them.
“There was a big dinner last night, and I was there and, and we had a talk, but he didn’t tell me that he had changed his plans for me.”
The Irish Whiskey Association said it “heartily welcomes” the announcement, stating: “We will continue to work with our EU and US counterparts to secure a return to the zero-for-zero arrangement for all drinks exports.”
Ireland’s deputy premier Simon Harris said it was a “welcome announcement of economic significance”.
He added: “This announcement coupled with the very significant and positive tourism exposure generated in recent days for our country has made this a consequential visit and a reminder of the importance of the economic relationship between Ireland and the US.”
On Saturday, Mr Trump sparked a row when he responded to a question from the Press Association, by saying he “would love to see” Ireland unified, adding: “It’s going to happen eventually.”
Mr Trump spoke to reporters on Sunday at his golf resort.
When asked about the diplomatic row after his comments the previous day, he said: “I loved them.”
Asked about the backlash he said: “I love my comments.”
He did not comment further when asked about a timeline for Irish unity.
Mr Trump also said it was “great” to be in Doonbeg and added: “I love Irish people.”
The president was cheered and applauded as he walked around his golf resort on Sunday.
Asked again about his comments on Irish unity, he said: “I have always loved the people of Ireland and it just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland and it would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is put them together.
“That’s only my opinion. Many people agree. I made what I considered to be a fairly routine comment, I have had so much support on that.”
Mr Trump said he would “say nothing” about Scottish independence, adding that he would “save that for another day”.
Asked about Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s remarks that there would be no poll on Irish unity until a majority in Northern Ireland were likely to vote in favour, Mr Trump added: “Everybody says that and then things happen.”
Taoiseach Mr Martin other senior Irish Government figures also attended the final day of play at the Irish Open.
Mr Martin said he had had lunch with the president on Sunday, but it had not been a “formal political meeting” and they had discussed investment in the area.
The Taoiseach said Mr Trump’s remarks in favour of Irish unity were “not a particular surprise” to him.
He added: “He would make the point that this is his view, he believes unity is the logical way for the island to be configured and organised.”
Asked about the political reaction to Mr Trump’s comments, Mr Martin added: “I think some of the reaction is an overreaction.
“It shouldn’t be a surprise he takes a different sort of perspective on things, we know that.
“Certainly he is viewing it, from my conversations with him over lunch, he is looking at it from a perspective of looking in on the island of Ireland and logically saying it seems inevitable it should be unified.”
He said: “That is his consistent view, he believes that and people are entitled to have a view and an opinion.”
A major security operation was in place for the visit, with Ireland’s police service An Garda Síochána liaising with the Defence Forces and US Secret Service in the area around the resort.
Mr Trump’s presence sparked protests in Dublin and Clare – but Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said there would be “no tolerance” of public disorder or attempts to impact “critical movements” of the US president.
A small number of protesters gathered close to Shannon Airport and in Doonbeg on Sunday.

sources.text:
If you're like me, you like the occasional dram before bedtime, or before supper, or after lunch, or whenever you feel like it - responsibly, of course. Never to excess, never when driving, and never, ever when handling firearms.
What's more, a lot of us are fond of really good Irish whiskey. The Irish may be known for Guinness, but they make some great whiskeys, too. The catch is that there has been a 10 percent tariff on Irish whiskey imported into the United States for some time now. But President Donald Trump, on a recent visit to the Emerald Isle, made a surprising promise: namely, to lift that tariff, making great Irish whiskeys a little more affordable over here.
That's good news and then some.
President Trump said Sunday that he plans to lift tariffs on Irish whiskey, an announcement he made while visiting the Emerald Isle.
“Ireland itself has been so incredible, so inviting, and we’re very honored by presenting you with a great course. It’s been great,” the president said while speaking at a ceremony for the Amgen Irish Open, a golf tournament, at the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg.
“I want to mention one thing, Taoiseach [Micheál Martin] and I talked about it, and [Irish golfer] Shane [Lowry] talked about it, and everybody’s been bugging me, they’re saying, ‘Would you do me a favor? It’s so unfair what’s going on. Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey?’ And I said, ‘On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off,’” he continued.
A dram of Tullamore Dew, Bushmills 12 Year Single Malt, or Jameson may be about to get a little more affordable.
This isn't the first time President Trump, a teetotaler himself (hey, nobody's perfect), has made our tipples a little more affordable; he's done it for Scotch, too.
Last April, Trump said that he was dropping tariffs on Scotch whisky after a visit from the U.K.’s King Charles III and Queen Camilla.
“I will be removing the Tariffs and Restrictions on Whiskey having to do with Scotland’s ability to work with the Commonwealth of Kentucky on Whiskey and Bourbon, two very important Industries within Scotland and Kentucky,” Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time.
He did remove the tariffs on Scotch, so there's no reason to believe he doesn't mean it for Irish whiskey. Work may be the curse of the drinking man, but at least being a drinking man, in these days of rising costs, may actually get a little bit cheaper, where whiskeys from Ireland and Scotland are concerned. Although I love a good Irish whiskey or Scotch now and then, my favorites at the moment are a couple of whiskeys distilled in Texas and sold under the brand (of course) TX; they have a nice bourbon and a lovely blended whiskey, with a buttery-smooth, mildly smoky flavor. Another of my favored blended whiskeys, as well, is made right up the road at the world-famous (in Alaska) Denali Distillery.
But it's good to have variety. And President Trump, while he may abstain himself, has shown he has a little bit of heart for his constituents who enjoy a good imported snort every now and then.

sources.text:
Donald Trump claims he will remove tariffs from Irish whiskey in Irish Open speech
US president Donald Trump made a surprise announcement that he was removing US tariffs on Irish whiskey as he brought his two-day visit to Ireland to a close.
Crowds cheered Mr Trump as he made the announcement on the 18th green during the prize-winning ceremony at the Amgen Irish Open at his Doonbeg golf resort in Co Clare.
He told the crowd he had discussed tariffs with Taoiseach Micheál Martin.
He said: “Everybody’s been bugging me. They are saying, 'Would you do me a favour? It’s so unfair what’s going on'.
“'Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey' and I said, on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey.”
Whiskey made in Ireland sold into the US is subject to a 10% tariff.
Lowry joked at a post-tournament press conference: “Irish distillers better be sending me a cheque soon — that must be worth a few quid with them.
“There was a big dinner last night, and I was there and, and we had a talk, but he didn’t tell me that he had changed his plans for me.”
Enterprise minister Peter Burke welcomed the announcement, saying that the US is a vital market for distillers in Ireland.
"This decision restores a fair playing field for Irish whiskey producers in the American market, protecting jobs across the country and strengthening our reputation for world-renowned food and drink production."
The Irish Whiskey Association (IWA) also said it "heartily welcomes" the removal of tariffs.
"Nothing exemplifies the US-Ireland trade relationship better than Irish whiskey," the IWA said on Sunday night.
"Last year, Irish whiskey exports to the USA were worth €450m, while Irish distillers collectively purchased €80m worth of US whiskey casks. This relationship represents thousands of jobs and millions in investment on both sides of the Atlantic, and the return to tariff-free trade for our Irish whiskey distillers will strengthen this success and lead to further growth and investment.
"We will continue to work with our EU and US counterparts to secure a return to the zero-for-zero arrangement for all drinks exports.
"The IWA would like to thank all those who advocated tirelessly for our sector, in Dublin, Brussels, Washington, DC, and elsewhere and look forward to seeing this announcement fully implemented."
The US president, wearing a white baseball cap with USA written on the front, presented the Irish Open trophy to winner Shane Lowry.
Shortly after, the US president left Shannon Airport aboard Air Force One to fly back to Washington. He travelled to the airport by helicopter from Doonbeg and posed for photographs with his family before boarding the plane to take him back to Washington.
Earlier on Sunday, Mr Trump doubled down on comments in support of Irish unity, stating it was “one of the naturals of all time” to put the two countries together.
Mr Trump also dismissed the diplomatic backlash to his remarks, insisting he “loved” his comments.
However, he refused to answer questions about a timeline for a border poll and also avoided a question about Scottish independence.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin said there had been an “overreaction” to the US president’s remarks.

sources.news_title: Crowd Roars As Trump Promises To End Whiskey Tariff
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has promised an end to the 15% tariff on Irish whiskey.
Trump was attending the Amgen Irish Open at his Trump International Golf Links resort in Doonbeg, County Clare — and he took the microphone at the contest’s close to present a trophy to Irish golfer Shane Lowry, who won the tournament.
“This is an honor. We’re so proud. The whole Doonbeg — and frankly, Ireland itself has been so incredible, so inviting, and we’re very honored presenting you with a great course, it’s been great,” Trump said, but then he pivoted.
“I want to mention one thing. Taoiseach and I talked about it, and Shane talked about it, and everybody’s been bugging me, they’re saying, ‘Would you do me a favor? It’s so unfair what’s going on. Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whisky?'”
The crowd roared with laughter, and Trump smiled before he continued, “And I said on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey.”
The crowd cheered so loud then that Trump was completely drowned out as he finished his sentence.
“Thank you,” Trump said, turning to Lowry and adding, “Shane, great job.”
Trump was not clear about when the tariffs — currently set at 15% as part of the flat tariffs against many European Union exports — would be lifted. Those tariffs took effect on July 1, 2026.
Previously the president lifted tariffs on whiskey made in the United Kingdom — including Scotland and Northern Ireland — claiming that he’d done so in response to a request in late April from Britain’s King Charles III and Queen Camilla, who had been visiting the White House at the time.
“The King and Queen got me to do something that nobody else was able to do, without hardly even asking!” Trump said at the time.
The zero-tariff policy on Scotch whisky took effect July 24, a change the Scotch Whisky Association welcomed as “welcome news for business on both sides of the Atlantic.”

sources.news_title: Trump says he is removing U.S. tariffs on Irish whiskey
sources.text:
Trump says he is removing U.S. tariffs on Irish whiskey
DOONBEG, Ireland – President Donald Trump said at the end of a visit to Ireland on Sunday that he would remove a 10% tariff on Irish whiskey, a duty that currently falls under those imposed on all European Union wine and spirit exports to the United States.
Trump made the announcement in front of a crowd of Irish golf fans at a tournament held at a course owned by his family. He met Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin on Saturday at the start of a 48-hour visit to the country.
“Taoiseach (Ireland’s Prime Minister) and I talked about it and Shane (golfer Shane Lowry) talked about it and everybody has been bugging me saying ‘would you do me a favor? It’s so unfair what’s going on. Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey?’ ” Trump said.
“And I said on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey,” he announced to loud cheers from the crowd.
Wine and spirits exports to the U.S. were included in a 15% tariff applied on most items under a EU-U.S. trade deal struck last year.
Subsequent new U.S. tariffs on 60 trading partners in July, including the EU, brought the rate down to 10%. The move was part of efforts to rebuild Trump’s near-global tariff wall after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down his initial duties.
The Irish Whiskey Association welcomed the announcement and said it would continue to work with its EU and U.S. counterparts to secure a return to the zero-for-zero tariff arrangement for all drinks exports.
“Nothing exemplifies the US-Ireland trade relationship better than Irish Whiskey,” IWA Director Eoin O Caitin said in a statement, adding that the lobby group looked forward to seeing the announcement fully implemented.
(Reporting by Bo Erickson in Doonbeg, Ireland, Padraic Halpin in Dublin and David Ljunggren in Ottawa; Editing by Sergio Non and Nick Zieminski)

sources.news_title: Trump says he will eliminate US tariffs on Irish whiskey
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said he would remove U.S. tariffs on Irish whiskey, announcing the move Sunday while attending a golf tournament at his family's course in western Ireland.
"On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off," Trump said to cheers from the crowd at the Irish Open's trophy celebration.
Irish whiskey and other goods from the European Union are generally subject to a 10% tariff under an adjusted rate following a Supreme Court ruling striking down earlier Trump levies.
Trump's decision was announced as Shane Lowry, a professional Irish golfer, won the Open in his home country. The declaration delivers a major victory to the Irish government and highlights the often shifting — and personal — approach to trade policy under the U.S. president. Trump has regularly turned to tariffs to push for concessions and punish nations that have bucked his interests; he has also eased levies to reward allies.
The decision, which Trump announced to roaring applause at his family's golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, came at the end of a two-day visit marked by the country's efforts to engage in delicate diplomacy and maintain warm relations with the U.S. president.
Unlike other European nations that have been targets for Trump and drew his criticism this weekend, Ireland generally has been able to avoid some of that fire. Still, trade issues have been a major flashpoint between Washington and Dublin, with Trump critical of Ireland's economic model that has attracted U.S. companies and drawn hefty tax revenues.
The Irish Whiskey Association "heartily welcomes" the news, Irish Whiskey Association Director Eoin Ó Cáitín said in a statement. "We will continue to work with our EU and US counterparts to secure a return to the zero-for-zero arrangement for all drinks exports."
Ireland's leaders rolled out the red carpet for Trump, treating him to pomp and pageantry even though he was not making an official state visit to the country. Trump was given gifts and treated to an honor guard as part of a charm offensive in Dublin on Saturday when he met with the president and prime minister.
Irish distillers had lobbied for a reduction in the duties. While whiskey distilled in the Republic of Ireland and imported into the U.S. has been subject to the 10% tariff, Scotch as well as whiskey produced in Northern Ireland currently does not face such levies as it benefits from the U.S.-U.K. trade deal.
On Sunday, Trump said he was besieged by requests to address the Irish whiskey levies during his short visit, including appeals from Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin and Lowry. The Taoiseach raised the issue of tariffs on Irish whiskey with Trump when they spoke Saturday in Dublin, according to a person familiar with the matter.
"Following President Trump's earlier action to remove tariffs on Scotch and all other U.K. whiskies, this announcement is another positive step toward reducing barriers to spirits trade," Distilled Spirits Council of the United States Chief Executive Officer Chris Swonger said in a statement.
The move will be a boost for Irish whiskey producers. The global Irish whiskey market faced a "challenging year," especially in the U.S., where Irish whiskey exports declined by 5% in 2025, according to Bord Bia, the Irish food board.
Tariffs had dealt another blow to the whiskey distillers, one of Ireland's largest and most historic indigenous industries. They had already been beset by oversupply, faltering U.S. demand and the soaring cost of everything from energy to labor.
Wine and spirits have frequently been caught in trade disputes since Trump was sworn into his second term in the White House.
After Trump imposed tariffs on steel and aluminum last year, the EU prepared a host of retaliatory levies, including one that targeted American whiskey; Trump, in turn, threatened to slap a 200% import tax on champagnes from France. A tit-for-tat trade spat between the U.S. and Canada also has seen provinces pulling American alcohol from store shelves.
Trump's Irish visit was not without controversy. The president in remarks Saturday said he would like to see a unified Ireland — comments that sparked blowback in Northern Ireland, which is part of the U.K.

sources.news_title: Trump to Remove 10% Tariff on Irish Whiskey
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said the United States would remove its 10% tariff on Irish whiskey during the trophy ceremony at the Irish Open in Doonbeg, Ireland. The Orlando Sentinel reported that he made the announcement after presenting the title to Shane Lowry, prompting whistles and cheers from spectators. The administration has not given a date for the change to take effect.
Trump said several people had pressed him on the duty, including Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin and golfers. The Orlando Sentinel reported that Lowry was among those he identified; the Financial Times also reported that Martin and Lowry had personally urged him to drop the tariff. That account is being retained as attributed reporting rather than presented as independently verified lobbying.
Implementation remains uncertain
The tariff currently applied to Irish whiskey is the standard 10% rate for most European Union imports, after a 15% rate was reduced in July, according to the Orlando Sentinel. A separate exemption for Ireland could face complications because trade policy for EU member states is handled at the European Commission level, the Brussels Signal reported. The formal timing of any U.S. action was not immediately available.
The policy also matters to producers in Northern Ireland. Irish whiskey has one geographic indication covering the island, and Northern Irish distillers with cross-border supply chains were excluded from the earlier U.K. tariff exemption and remained subject to EU duty rates, according to the Brussels Signal. The Orlando Sentinel reported that the U.K.'s zero-tariff policy for Scotch and spirits made in Northern Ireland took effect in July.
The sector entered the announcement under pressure
Irish whiskey exports fell 5% in 2025 to about €930 million, following pressure from tariffs and currency movements, according to Bord Bia figures cited in the Celtica market report. The same report said the number of operating distilleries rose from four in 2010 to nearly 50 by 2024, leaving the industry with substantial maturing inventory as demand in the U.S. weakened.
The Distilled Spirits Council of the United States welcomed Trump's announcement as a step toward reducing barriers for spirits businesses, the Orlando Sentinel reported. Eoin Ó Catháin, director of the Irish Whiskey Association, also welcomed the prospect of restoring tariff-free trade and said the group would continue pressing U.S. and EU counterparts, according to the Brussels Signal.

sources.news_title: Trump States Whiskey Tariff Removal For 'Just Ireland' Not EU
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump has said that his decision to remove tariffs on Irish whiskey will only apply to Ireland, and not the EU.
Prior to this, whiskey made in the Republic of Ireland which was sold to the US, was the subject of a 10% tariff, putting it at a disadvantage to Scotch and Northern Irish whiskey, which had no tariff.
Mr Trump's announcement, which came at the end of the Irish Open at his golf resort in Doonbeg yesterday, has been welcomed by the Irish Government, as well by representatives of the Irish Whiskey industry.
Speaking on the tarmac at Shannon Airport before returning to the USA on his Air Force One yesterday evening, President Trump was asked by reporters if this tariff shift would apply only to Ireland or across the EU, to which he replied: "Just Ireland".
"It was very unfair because others had the relief and they didn't, so I thought I'd do it. Actually, Shane [Lowry] asked me about it, too. A lot of people asked me".
It had been reported that Taoiseach Micheál Martin had raised the issue of tariffs on Irish whiskey with Mr Trump while speaking to him at Farmleigh yesterday, with Trump promising to look into it.
Mr Trump announced the removal of the tariff while speaking at the prizegiving ceremony for the Irish Open yesterday at his Doonbeg golf resort, which was won by Irish golfer, Shane Lowry.
"I want to mention one thing. Taoiseach and I talked about it and Shane talked about it and everyone has been bugging me saying 'would you do me a favour? It's so unfair what's going on. Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey?", he said.
"And I said on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey".
This was met with a huge round of applause from the crowd.
This move welcomed by Tánaiste, Simon Harris, who said: "A welcome announcement of economic significance from President Trump this evening that reflects the very positive engagement we've had with the US administration on tariffs over the 18 months".
Elsewhere, Director of the Irish Whiskey Association, Eoin Ó Catháin, called this move a vote of confidence in the industry and will be a "gamechanger", saying that it will bring the Irish sector back to full equity with scotch whiskey, its biggest competitor in the US market.
"This isn't solely attributable to tariffs," he stated, "but they have definitely played a role".
"In addition, the first half of this year our export figures were down just over 20%", he said. "I hope the zero tariff will be extended to all Irish drink exports".
He continued: "The US is our biggest market, it represents thousands of jobs, millions in investments and it has been under pressure, I suppose, over the last year and a bit because of that tariff.
"We're delighted to see it removed", he added. "We'll continue to work with all of our colleagues in the US, in Brussels, here in Dublin to ensure this full tariff liberalisation will take place" and the that the association: "like to see a return to the zero-for-zero trading arrangement for all of our drinks exports". (All quotes mentioned in this piece are according to RTÉ).

Donald Trump matters a lot to Mzansi and the rest of the world right now. Trump is changing the way America works – and how the world’s most powerful country deals with the rest of the world.
We’ll track what he does and connect the dots to your daily life.
Trump drops tariff on Irish whiskey
US President Donald Trump says he will remove tariffs on Irish whiskey.
Trump made the announcement during a golf tournament in Ireland at a course owned by his family.
He said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin and golfer Shane Lowry had spoken to him about the issue.

Trump then told the crowd that, on behalf of the United States, he would remove the tariff on Irish whiskey.
The Irish Whiskey Association welcomed the announcement and said it hoped the change would be put into place quickly.

Image source: File
Ramaphosa works on answer to Trump’s five demands
President Cyril Ramaphosa is working on his response to five demands from US President Donald Trump.
Trump’s message was delivered in Pretoria by US ambassador Leo Brent Bozell III on 26 August.
The demands reportedly include stronger protection for farmers and a call for South Africa to condemn the “Kill the Boer” chant.
Trump also wants South Africa to scrap its expropriation without compensation law and change black ownership rules for US investors.
He also wants South Africa to distance itself from countries such as Iran and show that it is truly non-aligned.
Ramaphosa’s office confirmed that he will reply, but did not say exactly when.
South Africa believes it has already made progress on some of Trump’s demands and Ramaphosa is expected to explain this in his response.
His answer could be important for the future of relations between South Africa and the US, including trade benefits under Agoa.
Image source: File
Trump promises Americans R80,000 each
US President Donald Trump says every adult American would get R80,000 if Republicans win both parts of Congress in November.
Trump made the promise at a Republican convention in Texas.
He said every adult US citizen would get $5,000, which is about R80,000.
Trump did not explain where the money would come from or how the plan would work.
He said the money would have to be spent inside the United States.
There are nearly 270 million adults in America, meaning the plan could cost about R20.8-trillion.
Democrats called the plan an empty promise. Questions have also been raised about whether such a payment would be legal.
Trump said the payout would only happen if Republicans win both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Image source: FIle
Trump gifts White House staff up to R720,000 each
US President Donald Trump gave large cash gifts to four White House staff members over Christmas.
Financial records show executive assistant Natalie Harp received about R720,000 from Trump.
Communications adviser Margo Martin and White House staff member Chamberlain Harris also received about R720,000 each.
Walt Nauta, who works in Oval Office operations, received about R320,000.
The gifts were listed in financial forms released by the Trump administration.
A White House official said Trump has a long history of giving Christmas gifts to people who work closely with him.
The official said the gifts were not connected to their government work and were allowed under legal and ethical rules.
Harp, Martin and Harris each earn about R2.4-million a year, while Nauta earns about R2.8-million.

Trump trade war with Canada gets worse
Donald Trump’s trade fight with Canada has grown after Canada placed new taxes on billions of dollars of US goods.
Canada’s new tariffs took effect on Tuesday and cover almost C$28-billion worth of American products.
Some of the tariffs are as high as 50%. They apply to goods including steel, furniture and clothing.
Canada brought in the tariffs after Trump placed new taxes on Canadian products such as cars, steel, aluminium, dairy and alcohol.
Trump has also threatened to stop US business with Canadian aircraft company Bombardier unless it moves manufacturing to the US.
Trade talks between the two countries broke down in August. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada was ready to return to talks when the US was ready.
Trump has also criticised Canada’s currency and posted a map showing Canada covered by the US flag.
The US and Canada do nearly $900-billion in trade with each other. Businesses on both sides are now preparing for the fight to continue.

Trump plans calls with Putin and Zelenskyy
US President Donald Trump plans to speak by phone with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday.
Trump is expected to speak to Putin first and then Zelenskyy, according to a US official.
The calls are expected after Trump receives an update from his envoys about the latest talks on the war in Ukraine.
Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on 6 September for talks with Zelenskyy.
After the first round of talks, Kushner said Trump was determined to bring the war to an end.
Zelenskyy said several rounds of talks would take place in Kyiv, including meetings involving France, the UK and Germany.
Witkoff and Kushner left Kyiv by train during the night of 6 to 7 September.

Trump gets his face on new US coin
Donald Trump has become the first living US president in 100 years to appear on American currency.
The US Mint released a special $1 coin featuring Trump’s face on Wednesday to mark America’s 250th anniversary.
The coin shows Trump alongside the words “LIBERTY” and “IN GOD WE TRUST”.
The coins went on sale in rolls of 25 for $61 and bags of 100 for $154.50. They were listed as out of stock online within hours.
Despite their gold colour, the coins do not contain real gold. They are mostly made from copper.
US law stops living people from appearing on paper money. But the Trump government says the law does not clearly stop a living president from appearing on the front of a coin.
The last living US president to appear on a coin was Calvin Coolidge in 1926.
Trump’s government has also previously announced plans for a $250 note featuring his face, but that would need a change in the law.

Trump says he will not force Iran peace talks
US President Donald Trump says he is not trying to force Iran back into peace talks.

He said America had almost total control of the Strait of Hormuz and claimed Iran’s economy was falling apart.

Lucy Harrison, 23, from Warrington in England, was shot in the chest on 10 January 2025 while visiting her father’s home in Prosper, near Dallas.
Police investigated the case as possible manslaughter. However, a grand jury decided not to charge her father, Kris Harrison.
An inquest in Cheshire heard that Lucy had a “big argument” with her father about Trump, who was preparing to begin his second term as president.
Her boyfriend, Sam Littler, told the court Lucy often became upset when her father spoke about owning a gun.
On the morning of the shooting, Lucy asked her father during the argument: “How would you feel if I was the girl in that situation and I’d been sexually assaulted?”
Littler said Kris Harrison replied that he had two other daughters living with him and it would not upset him that much. Lucy became upset and ran upstairs.
Later that day, shortly before Lucy and Littler were due to leave for the airport, her father took her into his bedroom. About 15 seconds later, Littler heard a loud bang.
He ran into the room and found Lucy lying on the floor. Her father was shouting for his wife.
In a statement read to the court, Kris Harrison said he had been showing Lucy his Glock 9mm handgun after they watched a news report about gun crime.
He said he bought the gun for “security” and kept it in his bedside cabinet.
He said he could not remember if his finger was on the trigger.
The inquest heard that Kris Harrison had previously struggled with alcohol and had been to rehab. He admitted drinking about 500ml of white wine on the day of the shooting.
Police officers said they could smell alcohol on his breath. CCTV footage showed he had bought two cartons of wine earlier that day.
His lawyers tried to argue that the coroner should step aside, claiming bias, but the coroner refused.
In a statement, Kris Harrison said he “fully accepted” the consequences of what happened.
Lucy’s mother described her daughter as “a real force of life” who loved debate and cared deeply about issues.

South Africa agricultural exports hit record despite drop in US sales
South Africa’s agricultural exports reached a record $15.1-billion in 2025, even though sales to the United States fell in the second half of the year.
The Agricultural Business Chamber of South Africa said exports were up 10% from the previous year, driven by higher production and better prices.
Exports to the US dropped after Washington introduced tariffs of up to 30% on some agricultural products. Shipments to the US fell 11% in the third quarter and 39% in the last three months of the year.
Despite this, strong harvests of maize, citrus, table grapes and wine helped push overall exports higher. More growth is expected this year as production volumes improve further.
“Production conditions look good, so exports could rise again,” said Wandile Sihlobo, the chamber’s chief economist.
Some South African products, including oranges and macadamia nuts, were later exempted from US tariffs. Producers and the government have also focused on finding new markets.
China signed agreements last year to import more South African fruit, and talks are under way that could allow duty-free access. South Korea has also agreed to allow South African table grapes for the first time in 20 years.
Africa has become South Africa’s biggest agricultural market. In the final quarter of 2025, 53% of agricultural exports went to African countries, up from 44% for the full year before.
Asia and the Middle East received 17% of exports in the last quarter, the European Union 14%, and the Americas, including the US, just 4%.
In total, South Africa exported $504-million worth of agricultural goods to the US in 2025, down 3% from the previous year.
Agriculture remains one of the strongest parts of South Africa’s economy, with exports rising for seven years in a row.
South Africa also imported $7.8-billion worth of agricultural products in 2025, mainly rice, palm oil, poultry and wheat.

Trump says Iran leader should be very worried

ANC figures warn new US ambassador may not be welcome in South Africa

“An ambassador is supposed to help relations between countries,” he said. “But this one is saying he’s coming here to force us to withdraw a legal case. That’s interference, and we can’t allow that.”
